issues.author: seanturner
issues.body:
Thom's comment:

    * A weaker example in my mind. Mostly requires a symmetric ratchet.
      Could work well with PSK-based approach (or maybe a deployment
      mechanism where the initial state is established while a drone is still

     * Weakness: closely related to defense applications, which may trigger
       pushback.

As discussed at 9 September meeting, look to reword text.

issues.title: Introduction: Comment
issues.author: seanturner
issues.body:
Introduction, penultimate paragraph contains:

    Connection resumption addresses a different problem. TLS 1.3 resumption
    with fresh ephemeral Diffie-Hellman can provide forward secrecy for new
    1-RTT application data, while PSK-only resumption and 0-RTT data have weaker
    security properties {{RFC8446}}. Resumption does not by itself recover from
    compromise if the attacker also obtained the resumption secret. Repeating
    connection establishment can also repeat the computation and bandwidth
    cost of post-quantum key exchange.

Thom wondered:

    Do you want to note that symmetric ratcheting is a useful mechanism here
    that TLS lacks?

Discussed during 9 September meeting:

    As discussed, we should note that ratchets is an option not the only option.
    Add the key update and regular update provides some features.

issues.title: Limitations of Current Solutions
issues.author: seanturner
issues.body:
Thom's comment on final paragraph:

    This paragraph suddenly suggests a solution exists before the
    properties of the solution were introduced. Probably makes
    sense for a later section that sketches it and then discusses
    these benchmarks.

issues.title: Security Considerations (1)
issues.author: seanturner
issues.body:
Carlos' thinks that maybe this paragraph is overly cautious:

    A resumed connection cannot claim post-compromise recovery if it is based on a
    resumption secret that the attacker still knows. A solution needs to specify
    how a compromised resumption state is invalidated.

issues.title: Security Considerations (2)
issues.author: seanturner
issues.body:
Carlos thought that the paragraph should be crisper by making it clear that the proposal is about 2 party and not 2 and more than 2 is dangerous. Suggested text follows:

    The scope is limited to connections between two endpoints.
    A third party that would contribute secret keying material,
    authenticate endpoint identities, or receive connection keys
    would change the trust model and require separate security
    and privacy analysis. One of the goals will those be to propose
    a solution that allows two endpoints to communicate but would
    prevent a third party to explicitly or implicitly also join the
    communication.

issues.title: Comments of the document.
issues.author: emanjon
issues.body:
I think this document is in a very good shape. I read the whole document and have the following comments / suggestions

...

>They do not introduce fresh keying material and therefore cannot restore security after that state has been compromised. Mechanisms that are currently being developed for TLS and QUIC to introduce fresh post-quantum keying material use an interactive exchange.

I found the post-quantum in the second sentence a bit strange.

>This document considers mechanisms through which either endpoint can independently initiate a key update that incorporates fresh randomness and can provide post-compromise security. 

Would be good to introduce post-compromise earlier

>Such updates can also distribute post-quantum update costs across a long-lived connection.

Not more that EKU. Would be better to state that "Intermittent connectivity, long propagation delays, and large post-quantum sizes make the property more valuable. "

>{{RFC8446}}

Should be 9846

>allows the connection to recover confidentiality

And integrity

>The property considered in this document is that either endpoint can independently initiate such an update without waiting for a live response from its peer.

I would remove "waiting for" or replace it with "the need for"

>Group key agreement is out of scope.

Maybe better with group communication?

>Key agreement that requires a request and a corresponding response before the initiator can complete the agreement and use the resulting keying material.

Maybe change "use" to "store" or "accept" based on comments last meeting

>Forward secrecy: : Protection of traffic from compromise of keying material at a later time. This property depends on deletion of traffic keys and the secret state from which they can be derived.

Also requires using different keys.

>Post-compromise security: : The property that a connection can restore confidentiality after an attacker has compromised its current key state, the attacker no longer has access to an endpoint, and a successful key update introduces fresh keying material that the attacker does not know.

I don't think PCS is strictly about confidentiality. Would be good to talk about the additional security the MLS signing gives.

Woulld be good to talk about the need to reauthentication without changes to the application layer

>A protocol can separately choose to fragment a single update across several messages.

Is that already specified? Otherwise should make sure to do that at the MLS or TLS/QUIC layer.

>five to fourteen seconds for lunar communications

This seems a bit unoptimized as the moon is no more than 1.4 light seconds away.

>and between just under one minute and twenty-three minutes between Earth and Mars depending on orbital positions

One minute seems wrong and twenty-three is not the worst case. Mars is between 3–22 light minutes away. One minute round trip seems impossible unless the you use Tachyons :)

>without completing such a live exchange at update time.

Should explain that update time does not mean "starting to use"

>A receive-only endpoint whose state was compromised needs fresh keying material that the attacker does not know.

Should explain that this requires a reauthentication.

>Limitations of Current Solutions

I think this should explain that reauthentication with these solutions require changes to the application protocol.

>support post-quantum key establishment and state whether authentication is classical, post-quantum, or hybrid.

My view is that something new like CURRENT should _only_ focus on PQC (standalone or hybrid) and optimize for that. I think quantum-vulnerable should be explicitly out of scope. It will have zero value in a few years when this is published, and any focus on quantum-vulnerable crypto might be bad for the protocol design.

>authenticate each endpoint and bind every update to the connection, the initiating endpoint, and the applicable key state.

Not sure all updates should be tied to the connection. The resulting session keys should be bound to the connection and update.

Can you start TLS/QUIC with an already established 2-party MLS groups. My answer would be yes.

Binding to the endpoint requires signatures. The document should talk more about the MLS signatures.

>allow a deployment to distribute complete post-quantum key updates throughout the life of a connection. A solution can also fragment one update across several messages, but fragmentation is a separate mechanism.

I think the fragmantion of signed post-quantum key updates is important. I think the mechanism for fragmentation should be specified during the work. For TLS you should be able to interleave a fragmentated signed post-quantum MLS key updates with application data. Otherwise the large update blocks application data transfer for a while.

>define key confirmation and the point at which each endpoint can use or delete a key state.

I think this need to be discussed also earlier.

>Recovery of traffic confidentiality does not restore peer authentication 
>An asynchronous protocol must authenticate updates and bind them to the correct connection, endpoint, direction, and key state.

I think these kind of things should be mentioned earlier.

>A resumed connection cannot claim post-compromise recovery if it is based on a resumption secret that the attacker still knows. A solution needs to specify how a compromised resumption state is invalidated.

Also here it would be good to discuss passive and active attackers.

comments.author: thomwiggers
comments.body: This whole paragraph text seems very "why doesn't TLS just work for you". If the traffic is so continuous, you can keep a TLS session alive; EKU solves the gap for rekeying.  Meanwhile if your log integrity is so important, you actually need synchronous acknowledgement of log entries to avoid truncation attacks. So using that as an argument actually weakens the argument that a CURRENT-approach works better imo.
